varieties.name: Green Globe
varieties.notes: The classic perennial globe artichoke; big green buds for years where winters are mild.

varieties.name: Imperial Star
varieties.notes: Bred to bud the first year from seed, so it can be grown as an annual where winters are too cold.

varieties.name: Violetto
varieties.notes: Italian purple artichoke with smaller, elongated buds; tender and good for frying whole.

varieties.name: Colorado Star
varieties.notes: Purple-budded variety that buds in its first year, so it works as an annual in cold-winter areas.

varieties.name: Big Heart
varieties.notes: Spineless plant with very large, round buds; easier to handle than spiny types.

varieties.name: Jersey Knight
varieties.notes: All-male hybrid with thick spears; vigorous and resistant to rust and fusarium. Widely adapted.

varieties.name: Jersey Giant
varieties.notes: All-male hybrid with heavy yields and good rust resistance; a cold-tolerant standard.

varieties.name: Jersey Supreme
varieties.notes: All-male hybrid that spears early and adapts to both cold and warmer climates.

varieties.name: Millennium
varieties.notes: Canadian all-male type bred for cold, short-season climates; long-lived and very productive.

varieties.name: UC 157
varieties.notes: California hybrid bred for mild winters and heat; the top choice where winters are warm.

varieties.name: Purple Passion
varieties.notes: Sweet purple spears that are tender enough to eat raw; turns green when cooked.

varieties.name: Mary Washington
varieties.notes: Old open-pollinated standard with rust resistance; cheaper crowns but lower yields than all-male hybrids.

varieties.name: Canada Red
varieties.notes: Red-stalked variety that stays red when cooked; sweet and tender, with few seed stalks.

varieties.name: Victoria
varieties.notes: Old reliable variety with green stalks blushed red; vigorous and heavy-yielding, often grown from seed.

varieties.name: Crimson Red
varieties.notes: Bright red stalks with tart, full flavor; a popular red variety sold as crowns.

varieties.name: Valentine
varieties.notes: Deep red, thick stalks that keep their color when cooked; good for sauces and pies.

varieties.name: Glaskins Perpetual
varieties.notes: Seed-grown type that can be picked lightly in year one and over a longer season; copes with warmer summers.

varieties.name: Maliner Kren
varieties.notes: Classic Bohemian horseradish with large, white, very pungent roots; the type most nurseries sell.

varieties.name: Bohemian
varieties.notes: General strain sold under this name; vigorous with smooth, hot roots. Few named varieties exist.

varieties.name: Variegata
varieties.notes: Ornamental cream-splashed leaves on a plant with usable roots; less aggressive spreader.

varieties.name: Stampede
varieties.notes: Matures early with large, knobby tubers; the best pick where summers are short.

varieties.name: Fuseau
varieties.notes: Long, smooth, spindle-shaped tubers that are much easier to clean and peel.

varieties.name: Red Fuseau
varieties.notes: Smooth, elongated tubers with rosy skin; easy to scrub and attractive on the plate.

varieties.name: Clearwater
varieties.notes: White, fairly smooth, rounded tubers on shorter plants; flowers less, so energy goes to tubers.

varieties.name: Albion
varieties.notes: Large, firm, sweet berries from spring to fall; handles heat better than most.

varieties.name: Seascape
varieties.notes: Reliable day-neutral that fruits all season, even on first-year plants; widely adapted.

varieties.name: San Andreas
varieties.notes: Sweet, firm berries over a long season with good disease resistance; Albion's sibling.

varieties.name: Tristar
varieties.notes: Small, very sweet berries all summer from a hardy plant; a good everbearer where winters are cold.

varieties.name: Chandler
varieties.notes: Large, flavorful berries; plant in fall in mild-winter regions for a big spring crop.

varieties.name: Sweet Charlie
varieties.notes: Very early, sweet berries bred in Florida for warm climates and fall planting.

varieties.name: Earliglow
varieties.notes: One of the earliest and best-flavored June-bearers, with strong disease resistance.

varieties.name: Honeoye
varieties.notes: Heavy crops of bright, tart-sweet berries on a very hardy plant; a cold-climate favorite.

varieties.name: Allstar
varieties.notes: Large, light-red, mild berries on a vigorous, disease-resistant plant; widely adapted.

varieties.name: Jewel
varieties.notes: Large, glossy, firm berries with excellent flavor; a top choice for freezing and fresh eating.

varieties.name: Sparkle
varieties.notes: Old favorite with soft, intensely flavored berries for jam; very hardy.

varieties.name: Ozark Beauty
varieties.notes: Classic everbearer: a June crop and a smaller late-summer crop of large, sweet berries.

varieties.name: Sunshine Blue
varieties.notes: Compact, evergreen-ish and self-fertile; one of the lowest-chill blueberries and great in containers.

varieties.name: Misty
varieties.notes: Low-chill, vigorous bush for mild winters; plant a second southern highbush for best crops.

varieties.name: Emerald
varieties.notes: Very large, firm berries on a vigorous low-chill bush; plant two varieties for best set.

varieties.name: O'Neal
varieties.notes: Big, high-quality early berries; a standard in warm climates. Plant two varieties for heavier crops.

varieties.name: Climax
varieties.notes: Early rabbiteye that ripens its crop in a short window; plant with another rabbiteye.

varieties.name: Premier
varieties.notes: Large, flavorful early rabbiteye; needs a second rabbiteye blooming at the same time.

varieties.name: Brightwell
varieties.notes: Productive, upright rabbiteye that blooms late enough to dodge frosts; plant two varieties.

varieties.name: Powderblue
varieties.notes: Vigorous, disease-resistant late rabbiteye with crack-resistant berries; needs a partner.

varieties.name: Tifblue
varieties.notes: The most productive rabbiteye and the standard others are judged by; pair with Powderblue.

varieties.name: Duke
varieties.notes: Heavy, reliable early crop of firm, mild berries; blooms late, so it dodges spring frosts.

varieties.name: Bluecrop
varieties.notes: The most widely grown highbush: dependable yields of firm, light-blue berries.

varieties.name: Patriot
varieties.notes: Very cold-hardy with large berries and tolerance of wet soils; good for zone 3–4 gardens.

varieties.name: Northblue
varieties.notes: Knee-high half-high bred in Minnesota; survives deep cold under snow and fits containers.

varieties.name: Chippewa
varieties.notes: Compact half-high with sweet, large berries; one of the hardiest for zone 3 gardens.

varieties.name: Kiowa
varieties.notes: Huge berries on thorny canes; the lowest-chill Arkansas blackberry, suited to hot, mild-winter areas.

varieties.name: Ouachita
varieties.notes: Thornless, upright canes with sweet, firm berries; low chill and widely adapted from the South north.

varieties.name: Natchez
varieties.notes: Early, very large, long berries on thornless canes; good in warm climates.

varieties.name: Arapaho
varieties.notes: Early, firm, small-seeded berries on upright thornless canes; good disease resistance.

varieties.name: Navaho
varieties.notes: Very sweet, firm berries over a long season on upright thornless canes; needs a cold winter.

varieties.name: Triple Crown
varieties.notes: Huge yields of large, sweet berries on vigorous semi-trailing canes; needs a trellis.

varieties.name: Prime-Ark Freedom
varieties.notes: First thornless primocane blackberry: fruits on first-year canes in late summer as well as on old canes.

varieties.name: Heritage
varieties.notes: The classic fall-bearing red: mow canes each winter for a big late-summer crop. Widely adapted.

varieties.name: Caroline
varieties.notes: Fall-bearer with bigger, more flavorful berries than Heritage and an earlier start.

varieties.name: Anne
varieties.notes: Pale golden, very sweet fall raspberries; a dessert favorite.

varieties.name: Bababerry
varieties.notes: Southern California selection with very low chill needs; one of few raspberries for hot, mild-winter areas.

varieties.name: Dorman Red
varieties.notes: Heat-tolerant trailing raspberry for the Southeast; mild flavor but reliable where others fail.

varieties.name: Boyne
varieties.notes: Very hardy summer-bearer with sweet, dark red berries; great for zone 3 gardens.

varieties.name: Latham
varieties.notes: Old, very hardy summer-bearer with good yields and some virus resistance.

varieties.name: Jewel
varieties.notes: Productive, disease-resistant black raspberry with glossy, rich-flavored fruit.

varieties.name: Raspberry Shortcake
varieties.notes: Thornless dwarf bush (2–3 ft) for containers and patios; sweet summer berries.

varieties.name: Concord
varieties.notes: The classic blue-black juice and jelly grape; hardy and tolerant of humid summers.

varieties.name: Marquette
varieties.notes: Minnesota wine grape hardy to about -30°F; the best red wine grape for very cold areas.

varieties.name: Frontenac
varieties.notes: Extremely hardy, disease-resistant wine and jelly grape for zone 3–4 gardens.

varieties.name: Somerset Seedless
varieties.notes: Very hardy red seedless table grape that ripens early; ideal where summers are short.

varieties.name: Reliance
varieties.notes: Hardy red seedless table grape with sweet, fruity flavor; dependable in cold, humid climates.

varieties.name: Himrod
varieties.notes: Early golden seedless table grape with honey-sweet flavor; moderately hardy.

varieties.name: Flame Seedless
varieties.notes: Crisp red seedless table grape for hot, dry summers; not cold-hardy or disease-tolerant in humid climates.

varieties.name: Thompson Seedless
varieties.notes: The classic green seedless grape and raisin grape; needs long, hot, dry summers.

varieties.name: Carlos
varieties.notes: Bronze, self-fertile muscadine; vigorous, disease-resistant and a good pollinizer for female types.

varieties.name: Triumph
varieties.notes: Early bronze self-fertile muscadine with good flavor; cold-hardy for a muscadine.

varieties.name: Supreme
varieties.notes: Very large, sweet black muscadine; female, so plant a self-fertile muscadine within 50 ft.

varieties.name: Anna
varieties.notes: Also sold as 'Ananasnaya'; sweet, aromatic kiwiberries. Needs an arguta male within about 50 ft.

varieties.name: Ken's Red
varieties.notes: Red-skinned, red-fleshed kiwiberries with sweet-tart flavor; needs an arguta male.

varieties.name: Geneva
varieties.notes: Early-ripening, very sweet kiwiberries; good where fall frost comes early. Needs an arguta male.

varieties.name: Issai
varieties.notes: Self-fertile and fruits young, on a smaller vine; less hardy than other argutas and crops better with a male.

varieties.name: Arctic Beauty
varieties.notes: Super-hardy species with pink-and-white leaves; female needs a kolomikta male (arguta males won't do).

varieties.name: Stevens
varieties.notes: The most widely planted variety: large, dark red berries on a vigorous, productive vine.

varieties.name: Early Black
varieties.notes: Small, very dark berries that ripen early; good where fall frost comes early.

varieties.name: Ben Lear
varieties.notes: Large, deep red early berries; best used fresh as they keep less well.

varieties.name: Howes
varieties.notes: Old late variety with firm berries that store exceptionally well.

varieties.name: Pilgrim
varieties.notes: Very large, purplish-red berries on a vigorous vine; heavy cropper.

varieties.name: Frederick
varieties.notes: Reliable, self-fertile purple hybrid with large, tangy-sweet fruit; the go-to in California.

varieties.name: Possum Purple
varieties.notes: Self-fertile purple passion fruit with sweet, aromatic pulp; vigorous and productive.

varieties.name: Black Knight
varieties.notes: Compact, self-fertile vine with dark purple fruit; manageable on small trellises and in large pots.

varieties.name: Incense
varieties.notes: Hardy hybrid with fragrant purple flowers; roots survive mild freezes and resprout. Sets best with a maypop nearby.

varieties.name: Maypop
varieties.notes: The native Passiflora incarnata; dies to the ground in winter and resprouts. Plant two seedlings to get fruit.

varieties.name: American Beauty
varieties.notes: Self-fertile red-fleshed variety with deep magenta pulp and good sweetness.

varieties.name: Dark Star
varieties.notes: Self-fertile, vigorous, with sweet red-purple flesh; a popular home-garden pick.

varieties.name: Vietnamese White
varieties.notes: The common white-fleshed type; self-fertile, vigorous and productive but mildly sweet.

varieties.name: Sugar Dragon
varieties.notes: Self-fertile red-fleshed variety known for very high sugar content.

varieties.name: Physical Graffiti
varieties.notes: Large fruit with pink-magenta flesh and excellent flavor; sets better with a second variety.

varieties.name: Yellow Dragon
varieties.notes: Selenicereus megalanthus: small, spiny yellow fruit, the sweetest dragon fruit; slow and self-fertile.

varieties.name: Red Lake
varieties.notes: Long-time standard red currant: big clusters of bright red, tart berries for jelly.

varieties.name: Rovada
varieties.notes: Very long clusters of large red berries that are easy to pick; heavy yields.

varieties.name: Jonkheer van Tets
varieties.notes: Early, heavy-bearing Dutch red currant with large, tart berries.

varieties.name: Pink Champagne
varieties.notes: Translucent pink berries that are sweeter than red currants; good for fresh eating.

varieties.name: Blanka
varieties.notes: Large, sweet, translucent white berries on a productive bush.

varieties.name: Consort
varieties.notes: Immune to white pine blister rust, so legal in many areas that restrict black currants.

varieties.name: Titania
varieties.notes: Large, rich-flavored black currants on a rust-resistant, productive bush.

varieties.name: Crandall
varieties.notes: Native clove currant with fragrant yellow flowers and sweet black fruit; tolerates more heat and drought.

varieties.name: Hinnonmaki Red
varieties.notes: Finnish variety with sweet-tart red berries and good mildew resistance; very hardy.

varieties.name: Hinnonmaki Yellow
varieties.notes: Sweet, apricot-flavored green-yellow berries; hardy and mildew-resistant.

varieties.name: Invicta
varieties.notes: Heavy crops of large green berries for cooking; strong mildew resistance.

varieties.name: Pixwell
varieties.notes: Very hardy old American variety with fewer thorns; berries hang away from the canes for easy picking.

varieties.name: Captivator
varieties.notes: Nearly thornless Canadian variety with sweet red berries and good mildew resistance.

varieties.name: Poorman
varieties.notes: Old American gooseberry with sweet red berries good for fresh eating; vigorous and productive.

varieties.name: Tundra
varieties.notes: Firm, flavorful berries that hold well; pollinate with 'Honey Bee' or 'Borealis'.

varieties.name: Borealis
varieties.notes: Large, sweet, soft berries on a compact bush; plant with 'Tundra' or 'Honey Bee'.

varieties.name: Indigo Gem
varieties.notes: Productive, vigorous bush with tangy berries; pair with 'Honey Bee' or another early bloomer.

varieties.name: Aurora
varieties.notes: Large, sweet berries on an upright bush; 'Honey Bee' is the usual partner.

varieties.name: Honey Bee
varieties.notes: Grown mainly as a pollinizer for 'Aurora', 'Tundra', 'Borealis' and 'Indigo Gem'; good fruit too.

varieties.name: Boreal Beauty
varieties.notes: Late-blooming, late-ripening type; plant with 'Boreal Beast' or 'Boreal Blizzard', which bloom at the same time.

varieties.name: Boreal Beast
varieties.notes: Late, large-fruited and vigorous; pollinizes 'Boreal Beauty' and 'Boreal Blizzard'.

varieties.name: Adams
varieties.notes: Old standard American elderberry with big clusters; plant two varieties for heavier crops.

varieties.name: York
varieties.notes: Largest berries and clusters of the American types; needs another variety nearby to fruit well.

varieties.name: Nova
varieties.notes: Early, sweet, large berries on a smaller bush; a good partner for 'York' or 'Adams'.

varieties.name: Johns
varieties.notes: Very vigorous, tall bush with large clusters; great for jelly and as a pollinizer.

varieties.name: Bob Gordon
varieties.notes: Missouri selection with very heavy crops; clusters hang down, which deters birds.

varieties.name: Wyldewood
varieties.notes: Oklahoma selection that flowers and ripens over a long season; does well in hot summers.

varieties.name: Ranch
varieties.notes: Compact, sturdy Missouri selection that tolerates poor soils; good for smaller yards.

varieties.name: Black Lace
varieties.notes: Ornamental S. nigra with dark lacy leaves and pink flowers; fruits best with another nigra nearby.

varieties.name: Regent
varieties.notes: Compact 4–6 ft saskatoon with sweet fruit; self-fertile and very hardy.

varieties.name: Smoky
varieties.notes: Classic Alberta saskatoon with sweet, fleshy fruit and heavy yields.

varieties.name: Northline
varieties.notes: Heavy cropper with large, sweet berries; suckers to form a hedge.

varieties.name: Thiessen
varieties.notes: Largest-fruited saskatoon with excellent flavor; tall, and ripens over a longer period.

varieties.name: Honeywood
varieties.notes: Blooms late, so it escapes spring frosts; large fruit in heavy clusters.

varieties.name: Autumn Brilliance
varieties.notes: Small ornamental tree with edible berries and brilliant red fall color; widely sold for landscapes.
